HTTP and application caching: a practical guide

Written by the docs team. Filed under performance. Share Tweet Email

Caching is the cheapest performance improvement available to most web systems, and also the easiest to get subtly wrong. This guide walks through the vocabulary, the mechanisms and the failure modes, from the headers a browser understands to the eviction policy of an in-process store.

What a cache does

A cache keeps a copy of a response so that a later request for the same resource can be answered without repeating the original work. The copy can live in the browser, in a shared proxy, in a content delivery network or inside the application itself. Each layer trades freshness for speed, and the skill in designing a caching policy lies in choosing how much staleness each resource can tolerate before users notice.

Freshness and validation

A stored response is fresh for a limited time, declared by the server with a lifetime in seconds. Once that time has passed the response is stale, and a cache should check with the origin before reusing it. The check is a conditional request that carries the validator received earlier; if nothing changed the origin answers with a short not-modified reply and the cache keeps its copy, saving the cost of the body.

Validators: entity tags and modification dates

An entity tag is an opaque string that identifies one version of a resource, while a modification date records when it last changed. Entity tags are more precise because two edits within the same second still produce different tags. A weak tag says the two versions are equivalent in meaning even if the bytes differ, which is enough for most text content but not for byte-range requests.

Cache keys and the vary header

A cache finds a stored response through a key, normally built from the method and the address. When the origin serves different content depending on a request header, such as the language or the encoding, it must list that header in the vary field so that the cache stores separate copies. Forgetting it is a classic bug: one visitor receives a page in another visitor's language.

Directives for shared and private caches

The private directive restricts a response to a single user's cache, which matters for pages showing personal data. The public directive allows shared caches to store responses that would otherwise be withheld, for instance when a request carried credentials. The no-store directive forbids any storing at all, and should be reserved for genuinely sensitive material because it gives up every benefit of caching.

Immutable assets and fingerprinting

Files that never change under a given name, such as scripts and style sheets whose names contain a hash of their content, can be cached for a year. When the content changes, so does the name, and pages simply reference the new one. This fingerprinting removes the need for validation entirely and lets the pages themselves stay short-lived while the heavy assets stay cached.

Stale content served while revalidating

Two extensions let a cache answer immediately with an expired copy while it refreshes in the background, or keep serving the expired copy when the origin is failing. The first hides revalidation latency from the visitor; the second turns an outage into a period of slightly old content. Both trade strict freshness for availability and are worth adopting for content that tolerates it.

Application-level caching

Inside the application, results of expensive computations and database queries are kept in a fast store keyed by their inputs. The hard part is invalidation: when the underlying data changes, every entry derived from it must disappear. Short lifetimes are the simplest safety net, explicit deletion on write the most precise, and tagging entries by the records they depend on sits between the two.

Eviction policies

A bounded cache must decide what to drop when it is full. Least recently used removes the entry untouched for longest and works well when recent access predicts future access. Least frequently used favours entries with a long history of hits, which resists scans that touch many items once. Adaptive policies combine the two signals and avoid the pathological cases of either.

Stampedes and request coalescing

When a popular entry expires, many requests may miss at once and all rush to recompute it, overloading the origin. Coalescing lets the first request do the work while the others wait for its result. Adding a small random variation to lifetimes also spreads expirations over time, so that entries created together do not all expire together.

Negative caching

Failures can be cached too. Remembering for a few seconds that a resource does not exist spares the origin from repeated lookups of missing items, which are common when crawlers or broken links hammer the same addresses. The lifetime must be short and the stored answer must clearly mark the resource as absent so that a newly created item becomes visible quickly.

Measuring a cache

The hit ratio, the share of requests answered from the cache, is the headline number, but it hides the cost of misses. Track latency separately for hits and misses, the size of the stored data, the eviction rate and the age of served entries. A rising eviction rate with a flat hit ratio means the cache is too small for its working set.

Testing caching behaviour

Caching bugs show up only under particular sequences of requests, so tests should replay realistic ones: a first request, a repeat within the lifetime, a repeat after expiry, a conditional request, and a request with a different vary header. Assertions on the response headers are as important as assertions on the body, since the headers are what instruct every cache on the path.

A short checklist

Give static assets fingerprinted names and a long lifetime. Give pages a short lifetime and a validator. Mark personal responses private. List every header the content varies on. Decide how each cached computation is invalidated before writing it. Watch the hit ratio and the eviction rate after every change, and keep the policy written down where the next person will find it.
